claim: At startup, Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md, auto memory, MCP tool names and skill descriptions from the session’s setup.
why: AGENTS.md can load in place of CLAUDE.md, and an output style or --append-system-prompt text can add to the startup load.
check: Run /context at startup to see which configured items occupy the window before work begins.
quote: CLAUDE.md, auto memory, MCP tool names, and skill descriptions all load into context.

claim: After compaction, invoked skill bodies are re-injected but capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens in total, with the oldest invoked skills dropped first.
why: The caps bound how much skill text can survive a compaction.
check: Check whether a workflow needs text beyond 5,000 tokens in a skill or relies on older invoked skills when their combined bodies exceed 25,000 tokens.
quote: Re-injected, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens total; oldest dropped first

claim: Truncation of an oversized skill after compaction keeps the start of the file, so the most important instructions belong at the top of SKILL.md.
why: Large skills are cut to fit the per-skill cap and only the beginning survives.
check: Check that critical rules in long SKILL.md files appear near the top, not buried at the end.
quote: Truncation keeps the start of the file, so put the most important instructions near the top of `SKILL.md`.

claim: After compaction, Claude Code revisits up to five files it read or edited, most recently modified first, and brings back only a path reference for any of those files over 5,000 tokens.
why: Anthropic’s Effective context engineering for AI agents describes the file selection by most recent access, while the Claude Code context-window guide describes it by most recent modification.
check: If a workflow needs exact file contents after compaction, check which files were reread and which show only as Referenced file.
quote: Right after compaction, Claude Code re-reads up to five of the files Claude has read or edited in the session, choosing the ones modified most recently. A file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference without its content, shown as `Referenced file` instead of `Read`.

claim: Compaction summarizes path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md with the message history, so move instructions that must persist to an unscoped rule or the project-root CLAUDE.md.
why: Claude Code re-injects project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules from disk and reloads path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md on demand.
check: Find must-always-hold rules placed in paths-scoped rule files or nested CLAUDE.md; they may vanish after compaction until a matching file is touched again.
quote: Path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files load into message history when Claude reads, writes, or edits their trigger file, so compaction summarizes them away with everything else.

claim: At compaction, Claude Code summarizes context added by earlier hooks and runs SessionStart hooks that match compact, adding their output to the compacted context.
why: Earlier hook context is part of the conversation Claude Code summarizes.
check: If a workflow needs hook-provided context re-injected after compaction, check for a SessionStart hook that matches compact.
quote: Claude Code runs them and adds their output to the compacted context

claim: /context gives a live per-category breakdown of context usage with optimization suggestions and shows which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files loaded; /memory opens those files.
why: The page's own visualization uses representative numbers, so /context is the way to measure a real session.
check: Measure a setup's fixed cost by running /context at session start rather than estimating from file sizes.
quote: run `/context` for a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions, including which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files loaded.

claim: In Claude Code, Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token context window.
why: Compaction works the same way at the larger limit, and plan and model configuration affect availability.
check: For long sessions, verify extended-context availability for the selected plan and model and check the configured window, especially for gateway aliases.
quote: Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token context window.

claim: Anthropic recommends running /clear when switching to unrelated work, because stale conversation crowds out needed files and costs tokens on every subsequent message.
why: Old conversation takes up room needed for the next task and costs tokens on each subsequent message.
check: Look for sessions that keep unrelated work in the same conversation after switching tasks.
quote: Old conversation crowds out the files you need next and costs tokens on every message.

claim: With auto memory enabled, Claude Code loads the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md at session start, whichever limit comes first.
why: Claude keeps the startup index concise by storing detailed notes in separate topic files.
check: Verify that auto memory is on and that any entries expected at startup fall within both MEMORY.md read limits.
quote: While auto memory is on, the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md`, whichever comes first, load at session start.

claim: When auto memory is on, Claude Code loads up to the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md at startup, whichever limit comes first, and reads topic files on demand with its file tools.
why: Keeping detail in topic files keeps the startup load small.
check: With auto memory enabled, check whether MEMORY.md keeps pointers to the topic files where the detailed notes belong.
quote: Claude Code doesn't load topic files such as `user_role.md` or `feedback_testing.md` at startup.

claim: Anthropic's size target for a CLAUDE.md file is under 200 lines, because longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.
why: The source ties file length to both token cost and instruction-following.
check: Measure each CLAUDE.md against the under-200-line target and use startup or /status warnings to check for oversized instruction files and imports.
quote: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.

claim: Splitting CLAUDE.md with @path imports organizes it but does not reduce context cost, because imported files load together with the importing file.
why: Imports are expanded into context at load time.
check: Do not credit a CLAUDE.md that is small only because it imports large files; count the imported text too.
quote: help you organize a long file but don't reduce its context cost, because imported files load together with the CLAUDE.md that imports them.

claim: CLAUDE.md @imports can nest to a maximum depth of four hops.
why: Recursion is bounded.
check: Check import chains deeper than four levels; deeper files will not load.
quote: Imported files can recursively import other files, with a maximum depth of four hops.

claim: Claude Code skips a launch-loaded CLAUDE.md over 4 MiB entirely and loads none of it.
why: The hard limit is far above the 200-line recommendation but loses everything rather than truncating.
check: Check whether any CLAUDE.md expected to load at launch exceeds 4 MiB and is therefore skipped.
quote: Claude Code skips a file over 4 MiB and loads none of it.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.309, Claude receives only the beginning of an on-demand instruction file that exceeds its per-file character limit.
why: The truncated content ends with a note telling Claude to read the rest, and later instructions stay out of context until Claude does so.
check: Measure nested CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files and their imports, nested rules, and path-scoped rules against 40,000 characters for 200K windows or, for 1M windows, 200,000 on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and 150,000 on later models.
quote: When a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` or a rules file that loads on demand is over a per-file size limit, Claude receives only the start of it. That part ends with a note telling Claude to read the rest with the Read tool, and until Claude chooses to, the later instructions aren't in its context.

claim: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md from the working directory and its ancestors at launch, from the root down, and loads subdirectory copies when Claude reads, writes or edits another file in that subdirectory.
why: Claude concatenates the ancestor files and appends CLAUDE.local.md after CLAUDE.md at each level.
check: In a monorepo, check which ancestor CLAUDE.md files load at launch and whether claudeMdExcludes is needed to skip other teams' files.
quote: Instead of loading them at launch, Claude Code loads each one once Claude reads, writes, or edits another file in that subdirectory.

claim: Claude Code strips block-level HTML comments outside code blocks when injecting CLAUDE.md, so those maintainer notes use no context tokens.
why: Comments inside code blocks are preserved, and comments are visible when Claude opens the file with Read.
check: Maintainer notes written as visible prose in CLAUDE.md are avoidable cost; they could be HTML comments.
quote: Block-level HTML comments (`<!-- maintainer notes -->`) in CLAUDE.md files are stripped before the content is injected

claim: With project settings enabled, Claude Code loads unscoped project rules at launch and path-scoped project rules when Claude works with a matching file.
why: Anthropic recommends skills for task-specific instructions that can wait until the skill is invoked or Claude determines it is relevant.
check: Check whether unscoped project rules load instructions needed only for particular paths or tasks, and whether the project settings source is enabled.
quote: Rules without [`paths` frontmatter](#path-specific-rules) are loaded at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

claim: CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt rather than as part of the system prompt, and carries no guarantee of strict compliance.
why: For actions that must run at specific lifecycle events, Anthropic recommends hooks, which run regardless of what Claude decides.
check: Check whether actions that must run before a commit or after a file edit rely solely on prose in CLAUDE.md.
quote: CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself.

claim: Claude Code warns at startup and in /status about individual instruction files over the recommended length, and warns at startup when files within that length together exceed a combined limit.
why: Each CLAUDE.md, rules file and @path import counts separately.
check: Ask for the /status output or startup warnings as direct evidence of oversized instruction files.
quote: If one of your instruction files is over the recommended length, you see a warning at startup and when you run `/status`.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.283, /doctor prompt-audit reviews instruction files for issues such as stale content, missing references or conflicts and proposes edits for approval.
why: The audit runs through the bundled /claude-api skill and is unavailable if that skill is disabled.
check: Run the audit with the skill enabled to review CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md and the rules, skills, commands, subagents and output styles under .claude/ and ~/.claude/ by default, or pass a specific path.
quote: run `/doctor prompt-audit` in a session. Claude looks for problems such as instructions written for older models, references to files or commands that don't exist, and files that contradict each other. You get a report of findings with proposed edits, and nothing in your files changes until you ask Claude to apply them.

claim: Where Claude Code supports direct AGENTS.md loading, a CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or an ancestor takes precedence by default.
why: Setting Project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md allows both types to load, and user and managed CLAUDE.md files do not block AGENTS.md.
check: Use /memory to check whether the expected AGENTS.md loaded and look for project CLAUDE.md variants or a Project instructions setting that explains its absence.
quote:
By default, Claude reads `AGENTS.md` only when you have no `CLAUDE.md` in your working directory or above it. Here's which of your files count for that check:

* **Count, so Claude reads them instead of `AGENTS.md`**: a `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, or `CLAUDE.local.md` in your working directory or any directory above it

claim: A SessionStart hook that prints AGENTS.md duplicates it once Claude reads AGENTS.md natively, and should be removed.
why: The same file would be in context twice.
check: Look for SessionStart hooks that print AGENTS.md in sessions where Claude Code already loads it directly.
quote: Once Claude reads `AGENTS.md` directly, the hook adds a second copy to the context.

claim: CLAUDE.md files from directories added with --add-dir are not loaded unless CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD is set.
why: Extra directories grant file access but not instruction loading by default.
check: If a setup expects instructions from --add-dir, check for CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 and verify the expected files, since path-scoped rules are excluded and CLAUDE.local.md also requires the local settings source.
quote: By default, CLAUDE.md files from these directories are not loaded.

claim: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), so what is in context matters as much as how much room is available.
why: Anthropic states a larger window is not automatically better.
check: Do not treat a 1M window as permission for bloated always-loaded context; judge each loaded piece by value.
quote: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as *context rot*.

claim: Prompt caching changes what cached tokens cost, not whether they occupy the context window.
why: Cached prefixes still count toward the window limit.
check: Count the cached prefix when checking how much context is available for the rest of a request.
quote: changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.

claim: The Claude API counts the system prompt, messages, tool definitions and generated output, including extended thinking, toward the context window.
why: Tool results, images and documents also count when they are included in messages.
check: Include system instructions, tool schemas, message content and expected output when checking whether a request fits the context window.
quote: Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message in `messages` (including tool results, images, and documents), and your tool definitions.

claim: On Claude Haiku 5.5 prompts over 100,000 tokens are billed at a higher rate, the exception to standard long-context pricing on 1M-window models.
why: Other 1M-window models bill long-context requests at standard pricing.
check: For setups using Haiku 5.5 for long sessions or subagents, check whether prompts regularly pass 100,000 tokens.
quote: except on Claude Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more.

claim: The Claude API counts previous thinking blocks toward the context window when it keeps them, which depends on the model’s default and any thinking block clearing override.
why: By default, the API keeps them on Opus 4.5 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5, 5.1 and 5.2, Mythos 5, 5.1 and 5.2, and Mythos Preview.
check: Check the selected model and any override, since earlier Opus and Sonnet models and Haiku through 4.5 strip returned thinking blocks by default.
quote:
The API keeps previous thinking blocks by default on these models, where those blocks count toward the context window like any other input tokens:

* Claude Opus 4.5 and later Opus models
* Claude Sonnet 4.6 and later Sonnet models
* Claude Haiku 5.5
* Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Fable 5
* Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5, and Claude Mythos Preview

claim: Anthropic's guiding principle for context is the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the likelihood of the desired outcome.
why: Attention is a finite budget that each added token depletes.
check: Check whether always-loaded tokens guide the expected behavior, and whether diverse examples could replace a long list of edge cases.
quote: good context engineering means finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome.

claim: Anthropic cautions that even larger context windows are likely to face relevance and context pollution problems when agents need peak performance.
why: Compaction, structured note-taking and multi-agent architectures can address context pollution over long tasks.
check: Challenge setups that justify large always-on context by pointing at a 1M window.
quote: context windows of all sizes will be subject to context pollution and information relevance concerns

claim: Claude Code uses a hybrid context strategy, loading startup CLAUDE.md instructions up front and using tools such as glob and grep to retrieve files on demand.
why: Up-front data gives speed and just-in-time retrieval avoids stale indexes.
check: Check which information needs to be available up front and which the agent can retrieve on demand.
quote: CLAUDE.md files are naively dropped into context up front, while primitives like glob and grep allow it to navigate its environment and retrieve files just-in-time

claim: Compaction is described as typically the first lever for long-horizon coherence, and tool result clearing as one of the safest, lightest-touch forms of it.
why: Raw tool results deep in history rarely need to be seen again.
check: For long agent sessions where raw tool results build up, consider whether compaction or clearing old tool results would preserve coherence.
quote: Compaction typically serves as the first lever in context engineering to drive better long-term coherence.

claim: Anthropic recommends tuning compaction prompts on complex agent traces, first maximizing recall of relevant details and then improving precision by removing excess content.
why: What to keep versus discard is the core difficulty.
check: Test a custom compaction prompt on complex traces for loss of relevant details, such as architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details.
quote: For engineers implementing compaction systems, we recommend carefully tuning your prompt on complex agent traces. Start by maximizing recall to ensure your compaction prompt captures every relevant piece of information from the trace, then iterate to improve precision by eliminating superfluous content.

claim: In Anthropic’s long-horizon architecture, a subagent may explore with tens of thousands of tokens or more and return a condensed summary, often 1,000–2,000 tokens.
why: Detailed search context stays isolated in the subagent.
check: Check whether subagents used for deep exploration return a summary that keeps raw research out of the lead agent’s context.
quote: returns only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens).

claim: Anthropic cites tool sets that cover too much functionality or make tool choice ambiguous as a common failure mode for agents.
why: Anthropic advises making each tool’s intended use clear and minimizing overlap between tools.
check: Look for overlapping MCP servers or tools with unclear boundaries and propose pruning.
quote: One of the most common failure modes we see is bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or lead to ambiguous decision points about which tool to use.

claim: Anthropic advises curating a few diverse canonical examples rather than stuffing a prompt with a laundry list of edge cases.
why: Examples act as pictures worth a thousand words; edge-case lists bloat the prompt.
check: Look for prompts trying to enumerate every possible rule and check whether diverse canonical examples convey the expected behavior.
quote: curate a set of diverse, canonical examples that effectively portray the expected behavior of the agent

claim: Claude Code re-sends the full context every request and caches by exact prefix match, so a change anywhere in the prefix recomputes everything after it and there is no per-file caching.
why: The model keeps no memory between requests.
check: When diagnosing a warm-cache miss, check what changed in earlier layers, such as the system prompt or tool definitions, before comparing reprocessed tokens.
quote: The match is exact, so a change anywhere in the prefix recomputes everything after it. There is no per-file or per-segment caching.

claim: Claude Code orders requests as system prompt and tool definitions, then project context, then conversation, to put content that rarely changes first.
why: An addition to the conversation leaves the earlier layers cached, and session start, /clear, and /compact are common points when project context changes.
check: Check whether frequently changing content is sent in an early layer where edits shorten the reusable prefix.
quote: To get the most out of prefix matching, Claude Code orders each request so content that rarely changes between turns comes first:

claim: Claude Code caches each model separately, so switching models recomputes the whole request even if its content matches, and each opusplan plan-mode toggle switches models.
why: Caches are model-scoped.
check: Look for model changes mid-task, including opusplan toggles and skill or command invocations in the main conversation that select a different model.
quote: each model has its own cache. Switching models recomputes the entire request even when the content is identical.

claim: When an inline skill or command’s model override applies and selects a different model, Claude Code sends the next request on that model with the full conversation history and no cache hits.
why: The session model resumes on the next prompt, and context: fork applies the override to the subagent, which uses its own cache.
check: Verify that a user-invoked inline skill or command actually switches the session model before attributing a cache miss to its model override.
quote: When a skill or command's [`model` value applies](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#frontmatter-reference) and differs from the session's current model, that turn is a model switch. The next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits. The session model resumes on your next prompt.

claim: Changing effort mid-session invalidates the cache on most models, with exceptions for Fable 5.1 and later, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 on API-key or Claude-subscription access.
why: Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, Claude apps gateways, disabled experimental betas and HIPAA configurations all use the cache-invalidating behavior.
check: Check the model, provider and configuration before predicting an effort-change miss, including that Fable 5.1 required Claude Code v2.1.260 for the exception.
quote: on most models, each effort level has its own cache, so changing effort mid-session recomputes the entire request.

claim: Anthropic advises picking model and effort at the top of a session and saving /compact for natural breaks between tasks.
why: Fewer mid-task changes mean a higher cache hit rate.
check: Look for needless changes to model or effort mid-task and consider natural breaks for /compact.
quote: Pick your model and effort level at the top of a session, then save `/compact` for natural breaks between tasks.

claim: Fast mode and standard speed keep separate caches, so Anthropic suggests enabling fast mode at session start to limit the history first read uncached at fast-mode rates.
why: Each speed toggle reads uncached whatever the other speed lacks.
check: Check the first fast-mode activation in long sessions and whether later toggles find a warm cache at the speed they switch to.
quote: To keep that cost small, turn it on at the start of a session.

claim: Claude Code keeps the original tool list when MCP tools are deferred, so connecting or disconnecting an MCP server mid-session preserves the cached prefix.
why: Changing upfront tool definitions invalidates the cache, with /advisor exempt because its definition sits after the cache breakpoint.
check: With tool search off or unavailable, check for added or deliberately removed definitions, and distinguish them from a dropped server whose definitions stay listed or a reconnect that adds WaitForMcpServers.
quote: Claude Code keeps the tool list from the conversation's first request for the whole conversation, so a server connecting or disconnecting mid-session doesn't disturb anything already cached. A server that finishes connecting after the first request supplies its tools as deferred definitions that Claude loads on demand.

claim: In Claude Code, changing a plugin’s skills, commands, agents, hooks, monitors or themes preserves the cached prefix because their content is appended to the conversation.
why: Appending leaves the prefix intact.
check: Check which components change and apply the MCP caching rules to plugins that provide MCP servers.
quote: It appends their content after the existing conversation, so the next request pays for that content and still reads everything before it from the cache.

claim: Compaction by design invalidates the conversation layer, and project context (CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules) is reloaded from disk and its cache rebuilt even when files are unchanged.
why: Project context is cached together with the conversation.
check: Account for the project-context cache rebuild and check whether compaction also replaces an outdated system prompt, for example in a resumed session.
quote: It's cached together with the conversation, so after `/compact` or automatic compaction its cache is rebuilt even if its files are unchanged.

claim: Claude Code’s /compact reads the prefix at cached rates while it is warm, but after a break longer than the cache lifetime the summarization request reprocesses the history as uncached input.
why: The summary request repeats the system prompt, tools and history.
check: Check whether planned compaction happens at a natural break while the cache is still warm.
quote: there is no cache left to read, so the summarization request reprocesses that history as uncached input.

claim: To abandon a path entirely, Anthropic recommends /rewind to an earlier turn, which restores a reusable prefix while the cache is warm.
why: The remaining history is the content the cache was built from.
check: Check whether users compact a path they mean to abandon and whether /rewind would return them to a still-cached prefix.
quote: Rewinding truncates back to a prefix that is already cached, rather than building a new one as compaction does.

claim: Mid-session edits to project-root or user-level CLAUDE.md preserve the cache and take effect on the next /clear, /compact or restart.
why: Claude Code holds startup copies in memory, while edits to on-demand instruction files can take effect if made before those files load.
check: When testing startup instruction edits, verify that Claude Code has reloaded them via /clear, /compact or a restart.
quote: When you edit your project-root or user-level CLAUDE.md mid-session, the cached prefix stays intact. Claude Code reads these files at session start and holds them in memory. To reload them, run `/clear` or `/compact`, or restart Claude Code.

claim: In Claude Code, permission-mode and output-style changes, skill and command invocations, and /recap preserve the cached prefix unless the action switches models.
why: These actions leave the existing request alone or append to it, with opusplan toggles and applicable inline model overrides as possible model switches.
check: Check whether an opusplan toggle or an applicable inline skill or command model override changed the main conversation’s model.
quote: These actions either append to the end of the conversation or don't touch the request at all.

claim: Removing old images or PDFs to stay under request limits rewrites the messages that held them, so the next request reprocesses the conversation from the earliest of those messages onward, one slow turn per batch.
why: Claude Code removes a batch of the oldest images at a time.
check: In screenshot-heavy sessions, check whether a cache miss starts at an older message whose image or PDF was removed, and reshare a removed file if Claude needs it.
quote: Removing images changes the messages that held them, so the next request reprocesses the conversation from the earliest of those messages onward.

claim: The first conversation after a Claude Code upgrade typically rebuilds the cache from the start because the system prompt or tool definitions change, and auto-updates apply at the next launch.
why: System prompt changes invalidate everything.
check: When diagnosing the first request of a new conversation after an upgrade, verify whether a system prompt or tool change explains the cache rebuild.
quote: A new Claude Code version typically updates the system prompt or tool definitions, so the first conversation you start after an upgrade builds its cache from the top.

claim: A cache hit refreshes the inactivity timer for the cached prefix, and the API’s 1-hour TTL charges more per write than its 5-minute TTL.
why: The longer TTL can avoid reprocessing after a break, but in bursts with gaps under five minutes its higher write rate buys unused cache time.
check: Compare idle gaps with the effective TTL and whether a longer TTL would avoid reprocessing a prefix.
quote: The time to live (TTL) controls how long a gap the cache survives. The API offers two: a five-minute TTL, and a [one-hour TTL](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching#1-hour-cache-duration) that keeps the cache warm through longer breaks

claim: Claude Code defaults to a one-hour cache TTL for the main conversation and some server-controlled helpers within subscription plan usage, and five minutes for other requests or billing modes.
why: The other-request bucket includes subagents, workflows, in-process teammates, forks, compaction and titles, and usage credits default to five minutes at the lower write rate.
check: Check the request bucket and billing mode, including usage credits, API keys and cloud providers, and verify whether a five-minute default or a supported override suits the idle gaps.
quote: Unless you choose a TTL yourself, Claude Code requests the one-hour TTL only on a Claude subscription

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.242, the main conversation and other requests have separate configurable cache TTLs, each accepting 5m or 1h.
why: In priority order Claude Code uses FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1, the bucket’s environment variable, its setting, eligible subagent frontmatter, ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1, or the bucket default.
check: Check CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL or promptCacheTtl for the main conversation and CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL or subagentPromptCacheTtl for other requests, plus experimental.cacheTtl from v2.1.248 for a subagent, where 1h is ignored on usage credits.
quote: Each control takes `5m` or `1h`, and Claude Code ignores any other value.

claim: A standalone subagent has its own cache prefix, and a fork of the current conversation inherits the parent’s prefix and can read its warm cache on its first request.
why: Prefix match requires an identical prefix.
check: When estimating cache costs, distinguish a fork of the current conversation from a skill using context: fork, which runs in a subagent with its own cache.
quote: A [fork](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#fork-the-current-conversation), by contrast, inherits the parent's system prompt, tools, and conversation history exactly, so its first request reads the parent's cache.

claim: Claude Code's cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory, because the system prompt embeds auto memory paths and the conversation opens with working directory, platform, shell and OS.
why: Different directories build different prefixes.
check: Do not expect cache sharing across worktrees or directories.
quote: In Claude Code, the cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory.

claim: Claude Code’s status line current_usage object exposes cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens, and a persistently high creation count can signal prefix changes.
why: A high ratio of cache reads to cache writes suggests healthy caching, and the API reports both counts per response.
check: Inspect current_usage in the status line for turn-by-turn read and creation counts, or use /usage from v2.1.251 for the main conversation’s session hit share and misses.
quote: A high read-to-creation ratio means caching is working well. If creation stays high turn after turn, something is changing in your prefix.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.251, /usage adds Prompt cache (main) after the first main-conversation API response, showing request count, cached input share, misses and cache state.
why: The main-conversation line counts compaction and tool-result clearing as expected rebuilds separately and shows that count only after the first one.
check: Use /usage for the main-conversation cache and check subagent cache behavior separately, for example with OpenTelemetry.
quote: After the main conversation's first API response, Claude Code also adds a `Prompt cache (main)` line to the Session block, summarizing the session's [prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md) use: the request count, the share of input tokens served from cache, cache misses, and whether the cache is warm right now. Requires Claude Code v2.1.251 or later.

claim: For main-conversation cache writes, Claude Code reports 1-hour and 5-minute token counts as ephemeral_1h_input_tokens and ephemeral_5m_input_tokens under usage.cache_creation in JSON output.
why: Claude Code reports writes split by TTL.
check: Run claude -p "hello" --output-format json and check which field reports written tokens when verifying a main-conversation TTL override.
quote: Claude Code reports one-hour cache writes under `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` and five-minute cache writes under `ephemeral_5m_input_tokens`.

claim: Behind a gateway that strips cache_control markers while returning success, the entire conversation history bills as uncached input on every turn.
why: Whether caching works through a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL depends on the gateway.
check: If repeated eligible requests through a gateway show no cache reads, check whether it forwards cache_control or flattens the marked system blocks.
quote: your entire conversation history bills as uncached input on every turn.

claim: Across enterprise Claude Code deployments, Anthropic reports around $13 per developer per active day and $150–250 per developer per month, with 90% of users under $30 per active day.
why: Costs vary widely with model, codebase size and usage patterns.
check: For a team spend estimate, establish a baseline with a small pilot before wider rollout.
quote: Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around \$13 per developer per active day and \$150-250 per developer per month

claim: The /usage Session block estimates cost locally from token counts using list prices or a managed modelPricing table, with a data-residency adjustment where applicable.
why: From Claude Code v2.1.211, /clear starts a new session and resets its totals.
check: In /usage under Session, check the Estimated cost line for the configured-rates note when contracted pricing is expected, and use the account’s billing source for actual charges.
quote: from token counts at list price, unless a [`modelPricing`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#modelpricing) table is in effect. An administrator sets one in your organization's managed settings so the figure uses your contracted rates, and while a table is in effect the `Estimated cost` line carries the note `at your organization's configured rates`.

claim: On Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise plans, the /usage breakdown recommends changes for behaviors that account for at least 10% of recent usage.
why: Shares show how much usage a row applies to, not how much would be saved, and can sum past 100%.
check: Use the recent usage shares to find items worth investigating and measure separately how much the proposed changes would save.
quote: Its breakdown recommends a change for behaviors behind 10% or more of your recent usage.

claim: Claude Code’s /insights analyzes up to 200 previously unseen recent local sessions per run, skipping very short ones, and writes its latest HTML report to ~/.claude/usage-data/report.html.
why: The analysis reports work patterns and friction, and its requests count against plan or API usage.
check: Use /insights for behavior patterns, /usage for token cost.
quote: A single run analyzes up to 200 sessions it hasn't seen before and skips very short ones.

claim: OpenTelemetry export works on every setup and is the only option that streams per-user token and cost metrics into your own stack in near real time; cloud-provider usage is not covered by Anthropic's analytics dashboards.
why: Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry billing lives in the cloud console.
check: For cloud-provider deployments, check that OTel or a gateway is configured if per-user cost is needed.
quote: works on every setup and is the only option that streams per-user token and cost metrics into your own observability stack in near real time.

claim: Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry counters claude_code.token.usage and claude_code.cost.usage increment after each API request and can be segmented by model and request attribution.
why: Attribution separates spend by skill, plugin and subagent type, and the token counter distinguishes input, output, cacheRead and cacheCreation.
check: Group by skill.name, plugin.name, agent.name or query_source as needed and, from v2.1.273, check OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 if actual names are required where defaults redact them.
quote: Attributing spend to specific skills, plugins, or subagent types via the `skill.name`, `plugin.name`, and `agent.name` attributes

claim: Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry input token count excludes cache reads and writes, which must be added separately to get total input.
why: Claude Code exports the API usage block as is.
check: For spans or events add input_tokens, cache_read_tokens and cache_creation_tokens, and for claude_code.token.usage add the input, cacheRead and cacheCreation types.
quote: so these values exclude tokens read from or written to the

claim: Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry cost figures are estimates, and official billing figures come from the Console, organization analytics or the cloud provider.
why: The client computes estimates using list prices by default, and a managed modelPricing table can supply contracted rates.
check: Reconcile telemetry cost against the billing source before citing dollar savings.
quote: Cost metrics are approximations. For official billing data, see

claim: The claude_code.compaction event records the auto or manual trigger, duration and approximate pre_tokens and post_tokens when compaction completes.
why: The compaction event exposes its frequency and context size, and api_request carries cost and token counts for individual requests.
check: Use compaction events for trigger and size, and use api_request with query_source compact for cost_usd and token counts, including cache_creation_5m_tokens and cache_creation_1h_tokens from v2.1.300 when the API reports them.
quote:
* `trigger`: `"auto"` or `"manual"`
* `success`: `"true"` or `"false"`
* `duration_ms`: Compaction duration
* `pre_tokens`: Approximate token count before compaction
* `post_tokens`: Approximate token count after compaction

claim: Claude Code requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 for OpenTelemetry export and ignores repository attempts to enable telemetry or choose its destination.
why: It prevents a repo from capturing content or redirecting data.
check: If export is missing, check managed settings, the launching shell or user settings for the enable and exporter variables, and check whether a repo selector disables a signal without a higher-priority override.
quote: Claude Code ignores the [OpenTelemetry exporter variables](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env) in a repository's `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`, so a repository can't use them to turn telemetry on, choose where it goes, or capture content.

claim: Claude Code defers MCP tool definitions by default where tool search is supported, initially loading tool names and server instructions.
why: CLI tools such as gh, aws and gcloud add no per-tool listing and can be more context-efficient.
check: Use /context to assess MCP overhead, look for unused servers in /mcp, and consider an available CLI that covers the needed workflow.
quote: so only tool names and server instructions enter context until Claude uses a specific tool.

claim: Anthropic recommends moving workflow-specific instructions from startup CLAUDE.md into on-demand skills and keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
why: Startup instruction text occupies context even during unrelated work, whereas a skill’s body loads when invoked.
check: Look for procedure-style sections in CLAUDE.md that apply to one task.
quote: those tokens are present even when

claim: Claude Code hooks can preprocess verbose data, for example by returning only ERROR lines from a large log or the last 100 lines of test output.
why: In Anthropic’s log example, filtering cuts context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.
check: Look for repeated verbose output and check whether the task can use filtered output without losing needed information.
quote: a hook can grep for `ERROR` and return only matching lines, reducing context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.

claim: Verbose work such as tests, documentation fetches and log processing should be delegated to subagents so only a summary returns, though the subagent's own requests still use quota and can be put on a smaller model.
why: Output stays in the subagent's context window.
check: For verbose operations delegated to subagents, verify that the main conversation receives a summary and consider a smaller model if it can handle the delegated task.
quote: Running tests, fetching documentation, or processing log files can consume significant context.

claim: Anthropic recommends the lower-cost Sonnet for most coding tasks and Opus for complex architecture or multi-step reasoning, and switching to Opus also changes subagents that inherit the session model.
why: Leaving Opus as the default is among the usual causes of unexpectedly high spend on API or cloud-provider plans.
check: Check the default model and whether subagents inherit an expensive one.
quote: Sonnet handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus.

claim: Claude Code enables extended thinking by default and bills thinking as output tokens, and default thinking budgets can be tens of thousands of tokens per request depending on the model.
why: Anthropic cites better performance on complex planning and reasoning tasks.
check: For simpler tasks, check effort first, use MAX_THINKING_TOKENS for fixed-budget models, and check whether thinking can be disabled, which is unavailable on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable models.
quote: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, and the default budget can be tens of thousands of tokens per request depending on the model.

claim: Anthropic estimates that agent teams use about 7x as many tokens as standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode.
why: Each teammate runs as a separate Claude instance with its own context and automatically loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills.
check: If agent teams are enabled, check team size, teammate model (Sonnet suggested) and shutdown discipline.
quote: Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode

claim: Claude Code sends the full conversation on each request, including tool-use rounds, and reprocesses the full context on the first message after the cache expires.
why: Even a short question in a long session incurs usage for the conversation, with cache hits billed at the cached token rate.
check: Look for long-lived sessions, /loop tasks or idle-triggered activity.
quote: Claude Code sends your full conversation with every request, and each time Claude uses tools it sends another request carrying that batch of tool results.

claim: Session-scoped scheduled tasks fire on their interval even while the session is idle and send the full context each time.
why: Each firing is a new request carrying the whole conversation.
check: Check /loop and scheduled tasks in large-context sessions, using the heaviest recent loops in the plan usage breakdown from v2.1.242 when available.
quote: fires on its interval even while the session is idle, sending your full context each time

claim: Compacting a large context is itself a large request, whereas /clear costs nothing, so when continuity is not needed clearing is cheaper.
why: /compact reads the conversation it summarizes.
check: Prefer /clear between unrelated tasks in the recommendations.
quote: When you want a fresh start instead of continuity, `/clear` costs nothing

claim: Anthropic recommends starting with cost levers that preserve output quality, such as caching, trimming unneeded tokens, auditing prompts and batching eligible work.
why: Batch processing trades latency for its discount, and context editing cost more than it saved on the measured short run.
check: Check for eligible quality-preserving changes before recommending tradeoffs in effort, budgets, model or architecture.
quote: **Free wins** cut spend without touching quality: prompt caching, token hygiene, a prompt audit against the model you are running, and

claim: Apply shortlisted API cost changes in Anthropic’s workflow order, starting with caching, input, loop and output hygiene, then batch, followed by effort and budgets, and finally model selection.
why: Savings rank guides which levers earn a change and how to allocate evaluation effort, while the workflow sequence determines when to apply them.
check: Check that caching stays on and that each selected change is applied and measured separately in workflow order.
quote: (free wins -> effort/budgets -> model), not in savings-rank order

claim: Cost should be judged per completed task, not per token, since a pricier model that finishes in fewer turns can be cheaper and a cheap model that fails still bills its tokens plus retries.
why: Per-token lists do not predict the ranking.
check: Reject cost arguments based on sticker price alone.
quote: API spend is optimized in units of **cost per completed task, not cost per token**.

claim: Anthropic’s cost workflow usually leaves model selection until last because it constrains capability, with an exception for an evaluation that explores model and effort together.
why: Checking a newer release in the same tier before stepping down can reveal lower cost, and switching mid-conversation cold-starts the cache.
check: When stepping down, verify that low effort on the current model meets the eval, then test one cheaper tier at a time from its own default effort.
quote: Model choice constrains the intelligence ceiling, which is why it comes after every lever

claim: Anthropic’s cost workflow requires an outcome evaluation covering a workload before applying a cost lever that trades capability for spend.
why: Without a relevant outcome check, cost measurements cannot show whether quality regressed.
check: Check whether the eval covers the affected traffic class, keeping tradeoffs as proposals where it does not and describing any free-win measurement there as cost-only.
quote: without one, savings cannot be told apart from regressions.

claim: Anthropic’s cost workflow uses roughly 10K tokens of tool schemas as a rule of thumb for considering tool search with deferred loading.
why: Search adds discovery overhead, so a smaller prefix can still cost more per task.
check: Measure schema size and test deferring rarely used definitions against an eval, including any added discovery turns.
quote: Pays once schemas run past roughly 10K tokens (MCP servers reach that fast); below that the search step is overhead.

claim: Anthropic recommends server-side context editing to free context space, with infrequent clears in large batches because each clear rewrites cached context.
why: Context editing cost more than it saved in the measured short run, and client-side pruning can invalidate later thinking blocks on models that enforce preserved-thinking checks.
check: Check that each clear frees enough space to justify rebuilding cached context and verify that any client-side pruning is compatible with the model’s thinking-block checks.
quote: **Context editing** (clearing old tool uses or thinking) **is a context-window tool, not a savings lever.**

claim: Anthropic recommends standalone subagents for self-contained steps with bulky tool results, returning a brief result while starting a separate prefix from the parent.
why: Isolation saves context but forgoes the parent's cache.
check: Check whether the deciding model needs intermediate results before delegating, and account for warming a separate prefix.
quote: note the subagent starts a fresh prefix with no cache shared with the parent.

claim: Anthropic recommends enabling prompt caching first because agentic API calls resend the growing conversation by default and quickly increase the amount of input processed.
why: The guide’s 40-turn example sends its first turn 40 times, illustrating roughly quadratic cost growth when each turn resends the growing history at full price.
check: Check whether repeated context is read from cache and use the model’s read rate when pricing it.
quote: A 40-turn task sends its first turn 40 times, so task cost grows with roughly the square of turn count.

claim: In Anthropic’s direct API sample, organization-days classified as agent loops had a median cache-read share of 84%, with the top 10% reading at least 94%.
why: The sample covered first-party traffic already using caching and classified loops using tool calls and results as a proxy.
check: Use a cache-read share below about 80% as a cue to investigate cache misses in a comparable workload.
quote: Over a full day of real traffic, agent loops read a median 84% of their input from the cache, and the top 10% of them, coding or not, read 94% or more

claim: Anthropic recommends appending changing per-request text after the last cache breakpoint in the newest user turn and leaving the text in earlier turns intact.
why: In the Sonnet 5 triage test, a changing 25-token status line at the front of the system prompt caused full rewrites, while appending it preserved cache reads.
check: Check whether timestamps, queue positions or similar per-request values change cached prefix bytes.
quote: Put per-request text, such as a status line, at the end of the newest user turn, after the last cache breakpoint. On later requests, leave each earlier turn as you sent it, with its old status line still in it.

claim: In Anthropic’s test on Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, system-prompt edits cost about 25 to 50 times as much as equivalent system messages, and top-level effort edits cost 20 to 40 times as much as per-message changes.
why: The test priced the prompt side of a request with about 100,000 cached tokens and accepted edits that can trigger a prefix-check error on the Claude API.
check: Where the model supports them, check whether mid-conversation system messages or per-message effort can make the change while preserving the cached prefix.
quote: Editing the system prompt cost about 25 to 50 times what the same text cost as a mid-conversation system message. Changing effort at the top level cost 20 to 40 times what changing it in a message cost

claim: For loops waiting on people, Anthropic suggests a 1-hour TTL when about 1 gap in 20 falls between 5 minutes and an hour and few gaps exceed an hour, subject to model-specific guidance.
why: The 1-hour cache writes at 2x input rather than 1.25x, and pauses over an hour expire both durations.
check: Check gap lengths and model pricing, including the measured break-even of about one turn in 30 for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 and the guide’s model-specific keep-alive cases.
quote: If your loop waits on a person between turns, use the [1-hour cache duration](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching#1-hour-cache-duration) once about 1 turn in 20 follows a pause between 5 minutes and an hour and few gaps run over an hour.

claim: In Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 test, adding a turn at 1-hour TTL to a conversation cached at 5 minutes rewrote the prompt once, costing $0.80 at 100,000 tokens versus $0.02 for a cached read.
why: The result concerns a switch from 5 minutes to 1 hour for a new turn, and the prompt-caching guide permits an earlier 1-hour breakpoint followed by a 5-minute tail.
check: Consider choosing the TTL at conversation start and use cache-write and cache-read counts to assess any planned mid-conversation switch.
quote: In Anthropic’s test, the first turn added at 1 hour to a conversation cached at 5 minutes wrote the whole prompt again, once: $0.80 USD at 100,000 tokens on Claude Opus 5.5, compared with $0.02 USD of input for a turn that read the cache

claim: In Anthropic’s Sonnet 5 triage test, changing effort and adding a tool cost $0.75 per session just after compaction, $0.92 on the triggering request, and $0.95 mid-session.
why: The triggering request still carried the full conversation, and Sonnet 5 used in the test did not run the prefix check.
check: Consider a natural break for a cache-invalidating change and check whether the model requires putting tool or system changes in messages to avoid a 400 even after compaction.
quote: Bar chart, cost per triage session: $0.81 USD no changes, $0.95 USD mid-session, $0.92 USD at compaction, $0.75 USD after

claim: In Anthropic’s Sonnet 5 triage test, loading all tools as the catalog grew from 7 to 502 raised cost from $0.55 to $1.02 per run, while tool search kept it at $0.56 for 502 tools with similar accuracy.
why: Every attached definition counts as input on every turn, and the measured job called only its two original tools.
check: Measure the cost of carrying rarely used schemas and test whether deferring them preserves task results.
quote: Line chart: with all tools loaded, run cost rises from $0.55 USD to $1.02 USD at 502 tools; tool search keeps it at $0.56 USD

claim: Anthropic recommends auditing prompts after model changes because legacy instructions can add work or hurt accuracy, as seen in its support-desk evaluation.
why: Removing verify twice reduced cost per ticket on Claude Opus 5, and removing a conflicting scratchpad improved accuracy on that evaluation.
check: Look for redundant verification, mandatory procedures, outdated settings and scratchpads, and check their effect on the current workload before removing them.
quote: Instructions the new model follows too literally cost money: removing “verify twice” cut Claude Opus 5’s cost per ticket, and removing “be maximally thorough” cut it almost as much.

claim: Before adding a second model, Anthropic recommends sweeping effort on the actual workload, with a separate session for each level.
why: Separate sessions avoid cache effects from top-level effort changes when they invalidate the prefix.
check: Compare pass rate and cost per task across effort levels, as in the Sonnet 5.5 SWE-bench Pro subset, where medium scored about seven points below high at about 59% of the cost per task.
quote: Sweep effort on your own workload before you add a second model.

claim: For tasks with a reliable failure signal, Anthropic recommends starting at low effort and rerunning only failed attempts at higher effort.
why: Computed on Opus 5.5 SWE-bench Pro subset runs, low with high retries solved about 97% at about $0.17 per task versus 95.3% at $0.29 at high throughout, including failed cheap attempts.
check: Check the verifier and price both attempts and the added wall-clock time on failures.
quote: run every task at a low setting and re-run only the failures at a higher one.

claim: Output tokens cost five times input tokens on Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1, and long answers carried forward in agent loops incur input charges on later turns.
why: Retained answers add input usage to every subsequent request that includes them.
check: Check whether a short answer meets the need, as in the Sonnet 5 triage test where a six-section memo cost 2.8 times the one-line answer at accuracy within run-to-run noise.
quote: Output tokens cost five times input tokens on Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.2, and Claude Fable 5.1, and in an agent loop every token the model writes comes back as input on every later turn

claim: Anthropic recommends Opus 5.5 at default medium effort for most agent workloads, Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning or long-horizon work, and Haiku 5.5 for high-volume work with checkable outputs.
why: On the SWE-bench Pro subset, Opus 5.5 at its default matched Fable 5.1 at its default within run-to-run noise at about a fifth of the cost per solved task.
check: Compare default Opus 5.5, cheaper candidates for checkable work and Fable 5.2 where needed, using cost per completed task and eval results.
quote: For most agent workloads, start with Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort (`medium`).

claim: Anthropic recommends tuning a single model first, and its delegation tests favored orchestration only for routine work with a long cost tail or work exceeding one context window.
why: In the measured dependent chains or work that fit one context without a long cost tail, the orchestrator’s model alone at lower effort came out ahead.
check: Sweep single-model effort before testing orchestration and compare cost and quality on work that exceeds one context window or has a long cost tail.
quote: In Anthropic’s measurements, delegation came out ahead in only two situations:

claim: Batch processing takes 50% off every token including cached ones for results within 24 hours, and is the second-largest free lever after caching for unattended work.
why: It trades latency for the discount and does not combine with fast mode.
check: For unattended jobs or evals, check whether results can wait and whether fast mode, message threads or Claude Managed Agents sessions rule out Batch API use.
quote: The Batch API takes 50% off every token of a request, including cached ones, in exchange for results arriving any time within 24 hours.

claim: Prompt caching matches exact request bytes in tools, system and messages order, so changes invalidate matching from the first changed byte through subsequent breakpoints.
why: A changing timestamp, UUID, JSON key order or tool list can shorten the reusable prefix when it changes bytes before the breakpoint.
check: Compare overlapping rendered prefixes to see whether per-request fields, serialization or tool selection make them differ.
quote: Prompt caching is a prefix match. Any change anywhere in the prefix invalidates everything after it.**

claim: Cache lifetime runs from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, so generation time counts against the TTL.
why: In the guide’s same-prefix example, a write and one hit cover the 5-minute write premium, while the 1-hour entry needs a write and at least two hits.
check: Use start-to-start gaps for requests sharing a prefix, and compare expected reads at the model’s rate before choosing a TTL.
quote: The lifetime is measured from the **start** of the request that writes or reads the entry - generation time counts against it

claim: Anthropic recommends checking cache_read_input_tokens after prompt-assembly changes because cache regressions can raise bills even when requests succeed.
why: The usage fields show whether cache hits occurred, and input_tokens counts only the uncached remainder.
check: After changing prompt assembly, verify usage with a repeat request that can reuse an identical cached prefix, or use standing cache-read monitoring.
quote: The costliest caching failure in production is silent: requests keep succeeding, the bill is just higher - no error, nothing announces it.

claim: An advisor can help only when the executor consults it.
why: The advisor definition adds input cost even when it is never called, and the measured pairings that rarely or never consulted showed no clear improvement.
check: Measure advisor consult rate and compare cost and quality with the executor alone across effort levels.
quote: An advisor can help only when the executor consults it.
